title: Software Development
summary: Learn how professional software is really made: requirements, design, clean code, Git, testing, debugging, agile teamwork, CI/CD and growing your career, with hands-on Python exercises.

modules.title: The big picture: from idea to plan

lessons.title: What is software development? The SDLC
lessons.summary: See the whole life of a software product, from idea to retirement, and the main process models.

slides.title: More than writing code
slides.text:
Software development is **solving problems with software**, as a team, over time.
Coding is maybe a third of the job. The rest: understanding, designing, testing, shipping, maintaining.
slides.narration: Many beginners think software development means typing code. In reality, professional developers spend a lot of time understanding problems, talking with people, designing, testing, and looking after software that already exists. Code is the tool, not the goal.

slides.title: The life cycle
slides.text:
The **SDLC** (Software Development Life Cycle):
1. Plan
2. Requirements
3. Design
4. Build
5. Test
6. Release
7. Maintain
slides.narration: The software development life cycle names the stages every product goes through. You plan, gather requirements, design, build, test, release and then maintain. Maintenance is the longest stage, often many years.

slides.title: Waterfall
slides.text: Each phase finishes before the next starts. Good when requirements are **fixed and known**; risky when they change.
slides.narration: The waterfall model runs the stages one after another, like water falling down steps. It works when requirements are stable, for example in some regulated or hardware projects. Its weakness is that users only see the product at the very end, when changes are expensive.

slides.title: Iterative and agile
slides.text: Go around the cycle in **short loops** (1 to 4 weeks). Deliver something usable each time, learn, adjust.
slides.narration: Most teams today work iteratively. They go through the whole cycle in short loops, delivering a small working piece each time. Users give feedback early, and the plan adapts. This is the heart of agile, which we will study later in the course.

slides.title: Roles on a team
slides.text:
- **Product manager**: what and why
- **Designer**: how it feels
- **Developers**: build it
- **QA / testers**: does it work?
- **DevOps / platform / SRE**: run it reliably
slides.narration: Software is a team sport. A product manager decides what to build and why. Designers shape the experience. Developers build it. Testers and quality engineers check it. Platform and reliability engineers keep it running. In small teams one person may wear several hats.

lessons.notes:
## The Software Development Life Cycle

| Phase | Key question | Typical output |
|-------|--------------|----------------|
| Plan | Is it worth doing? | Goals, budget, timeline |
| Requirements | What must it do? | User stories, acceptance criteria |
| Design | How will it work? | Architecture, data model, UI mock-ups |
| Build | Write it | Code, reviews, commits |
| Test | Does it work? | Automated tests, bug reports |
| Release | Get it to users | Deployment, release notes |
| Maintain | Keep it healthy | Bug fixes, updates, new features |

## Process models

- **Waterfall**: linear, phase by phase. Predictable but slow to react to change.
- **V-model**: waterfall where each build phase has a matching test phase.
- **Iterative / incremental**: build in small pieces and improve each loop.
- **Agile** (Scrum, Kanban): short iterations, close customer collaboration, continuous improvement.
- **DevOps**: development and operations work together; automation lets teams release many times a day.

## Why so much emphasis on maintenance?

Most of a program's cost comes **after** the first release. Code is read far more often than it is written. That is why later lessons focus on clean code, tests, version control and documentation: they make maintenance cheaper.

## Software development in 2026

AI coding assistants are now a normal part of the toolbox. They can draft code, tests and documentation quickly, but developers remain responsible for understanding, reviewing and testing everything that ships. The fundamentals in this course are exactly what lets you judge whether generated code is right.

quiz.q: Which SDLC phase usually lasts the longest?
quiz.explain: Software is maintained for years after its first release.

quiz.q: When does waterfall fit best?
options: When requirements are fixed and well understood
quiz.explain: Waterfall is predictable when change is unlikely.

quiz.q: What is the core idea of iterative development?
options: Write all code first, test at the end
Deliver small working pieces in short loops and adapt
quiz.explain: Short loops give early feedback and reduce risk.

lessons.task:
Pick an app you use every day (for example a messaging or banking app).
1. For each SDLC phase, write one sentence about what probably happened for that app.
2. Name which roles (PM, designer, developer, QA, SRE) were involved in each phase.
3. Decide whether its team more likely used waterfall or agile, and explain why.

lessons.title: Requirements and user stories
lessons.summary: Turn vague wishes into clear, testable requirements with user stories and acceptance criteria.

slides.title: Why requirements matter
slides.text: Most failed projects did not fail at coding. They built **the wrong thing**.
slides.narration: Studies of failed software projects keep finding the same cause: the team built something nobody actually needed, or misunderstood what was needed. Good requirements are the cheapest bug fix there is, because fixing a misunderstanding on paper costs almost nothing.

slides.title: Functional and non-functional
slides.text:
- **Functional**: what the system does ("users can reset their password")
- **Non-functional**: how well ("page loads in under 2 s", "works with a screen reader", "99.9% uptime")
slides.narration: Requirements come in two flavours. Functional requirements describe behaviour, things the system does. Non functional requirements describe qualities such as speed, security, accessibility and reliability. Forgetting the second kind is a classic mistake.

slides.title: User stories
slides.text: As a **role**, I want **goal**, so that **benefit**.
slides.code:
As a library member,
I want to renew a book online,
so that I don't have to visit the library.
slides.narration: Agile teams usually write requirements as user stories. A story names who wants something, what they want and why. The why is important, because it lets the team find a better solution than the one first imagined.

slides.title: Acceptance criteria
slides.text: Concrete, **testable** conditions. Often written as **Given / When / Then**.
slides.code:
Given I have a book due in 3 days
When I click "Renew"
Then the due date moves 14 days later

Given the book is reserved by someone else
When I click "Renew"
Then I see "This book cannot be renewed"
slides.narration: A story is not finished until we agree how to check it. Acceptance criteria are concrete conditions, often written as given, when, then. Each one can become an automated test later.

slides.title: Gathering requirements
slides.text:
- **Talk to real users**; watch them work
- Ask "why?" until you reach the real need
- Write down **edge cases**
- Prioritise: **MoSCoW** (Must, Should, Could, Won't)
slides.narration: To find requirements, talk to real users and watch how they work today. Keep asking why until you reach the real need. Write down edge cases, the unusual situations. Then prioritise, for example with MoSCoW, so the team builds the most valuable things first.

lessons.notes:
## What makes a good requirement?

A good requirement is:

- **Clear**: one interpretation only. "Fast" is vague; "search results in under 1 second for 95% of requests" is clear.
- **Testable**: you can check if it is met.
- **Necessary**: it serves a real user need.
- **Feasible**: possible within time and budget.

## User stories: the INVEST checklist

| Letter | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| I | Independent of other stories |
| N | Negotiable, not a contract |
| V | Valuable to a user |
| E | Estimable |
| S | Small enough for one iteration |
| T | Testable |

## Acceptance criteria example

```
Story: As a shopper, I want to apply a discount code,
       so that I pay less.

Given a valid code "SAVE10" and a cart of 50.00
When I apply the code
Then the total is 45.00

Given an expired code
When I apply it
Then I see "This code has expired" and the total does not change
```

## Edge cases to always ask about

Empty input, very large input, duplicates, wrong formats, no network, two users editing at once, time zones, different languages and accessibility needs.

## Where requirements live

Small teams keep stories in an issue tracker (GitHub Issues, Jira, Linear, GitLab). Each story links to its design, code changes and tests, so anyone can see why a piece of code exists.

## Small exercise mindset

Requirements are like the tests in this course: a precise statement of input and expected output. The exercise below asks you to turn written rules into exact behaviour.

quiz.q: Which is a non-functional requirement?
quiz.explain: Response time is a quality attribute, so it is non-functional.

quiz.q: In "As a role, I want goal, so that benefit", why include the benefit?
options: It explains the real need so the team can find the best solution
quiz.explain: Knowing why lets the team propose better solutions.

quiz.q: What is the main property of good acceptance criteria?
options: They are written by the CEO
quiz.explain: You must be able to check objectively whether they pass.

exercise.title: Check a user story
exercise.prompt:
A team writes stories in the form `As a ..., I want ..., so that ...`.

Read **one line** from standard input. Print `VALID` if the line:
1. starts with `As a ` or `As an `,
2. contains `, I want ` after that,
3. contains `, so that ` after the "I want" part.

Otherwise print `INVALID`. Matching is case-sensitive.

Example input: `As a reader, I want dark mode, so that my eyes rest.` prints `VALID`.
exercise.starter:
line = input()
# check the three rules and print VALID or INVALID
exercise.solution:
line = input()
ok = False
if line.startswith('As a ') or line.startswith('As an '):
    i = line.find(', I want ')
    if i != -1 and line.find(', so that ', i + 1) != -1:
        ok = True
print('VALID' if ok else 'INVALID')

tests.input: As a reader, I want dark mode, so that my eyes rest.
As an admin, I want to ban spammers, so that the forum stays useful.
I want dark mode, so that my eyes rest.
As a reader, so that my eyes rest, I want dark mode.
As a user, I want everything

lessons.title: Software design and architecture
lessons.summary: Learn how to split a system into parts with clear responsibilities, and the common architecture styles.

slides.title: What is design?
slides.text: Deciding **how the parts fit together** before (and while) you build. Good design makes change **easy and safe**.
slides.narration: Design is about structure: what the main parts of a system are, what each one is responsible for, and how they talk to each other. The goal of good design is not beauty, it is making future changes easy and safe.

slides.title: Cohesion and coupling
slides.text:
- **High cohesion**: each module does one job well
- **Low coupling**: modules depend on each other as little as possible
slides.narration: Two words sum up most design advice. Cohesion means things that belong together live together. Coupling means how much one part depends on another. Aim for high cohesion and low coupling, so you can change one part without breaking five others.

slides.title: SOLID in one line each
slides.text:
- **S**ingle responsibility
- **O**pen for extension, closed for modification
- **L**iskov substitution
- **I**nterface segregation
- **D**ependency inversion
slides.narration: SOLID is a famous set of five principles for object oriented design. A class should have one reason to change. You should extend behaviour without editing working code. Subtypes must be usable wherever their parent is. Prefer small focused interfaces. And depend on abstractions, not concrete details.

slides.title: Layers
slides.text: Separate **presentation**, **business logic** and **data access**.
slides.narration: A simple and very common structure is layers. The presentation layer talks to users. The business layer holds the rules. The data layer talks to the database. Each layer only calls the one below it, so you could swap the user interface or the database without touching the rules.

slides.title: Architecture styles
slides.text:
- **Modular monolith**: one deployable, clean modules (great default)
- **Microservices**: many small services; powerful but complex
- **Event-driven**: parts react to events
- **Serverless**: functions run on demand
slides.narration: At a larger scale we talk about architecture. A well structured monolith is the best starting point for most teams. Microservices split a system into independently deployed services, which helps very large organisations but adds a lot of complexity. Event driven and serverless styles are also common.

slides.title: Draw it
slides.text: Use simple diagrams: **C4 model** (Context, Containers, Components, Code). Record big choices in **ADRs**.
slides.narration: Communicate design with simple diagrams. The C4 model zooms from the whole system in its context, to containers like apps and databases, down to components. When you make an important decision, write a short architecture decision record explaining what you chose and why.

lessons.notes:
## Design principles to remember

- **Separation of concerns**: each part handles one concern (UI, rules, storage).
- **DRY** (Don't Repeat Yourself): one source of truth for each piece of knowledge.
- **KISS** (Keep It Simple): the simplest design that works.
- **YAGNI** (You Aren't Gonna Need It): do not build for imagined future needs.
- **High cohesion, low coupling**.
- **SOLID** for object-oriented code.

## Dependency inversion example

```python
class EmailSender:
    def send(self, to, text): ...

class FakeSender:          # used in tests
    def __init__(self): self.sent = []
    def send(self, to, text): self.sent.append((to, text))

class SignupService:
    def __init__(self, sender):   # depends on "something with send()"
        self.sender = sender
    def register(self, email):
        self.sender.send(email, "Welcome!")
```

Because `SignupService` receives its sender, we can pass a fake in tests and a real email sender in production.

## Monolith or microservices?

| | Modular monolith | Microservices |
|--|------------------|---------------|
| Deploy | One unit | Many units |
| Team size | Small to medium | Many teams |
| Complexity | Lower | Higher (network, monitoring, data consistency) |
| Start here? | Usually yes | Only with a clear need |

## Architecture Decision Record (ADR)

```
# ADR 3: Use PostgreSQL
Status: accepted
Context: we need relational data and transactions.
Decision: PostgreSQL 17, managed hosting.
Consequences: team must learn SQL migrations.
```

Short ADRs stored in the repository explain *why* the system looks the way it does years later.

quiz.q: What do we aim for in good design?
quiz.explain: Focused modules with few dependencies are easiest to change.

quiz.q: What does YAGNI advise?
options: Build every feature you might need
Do not build for imagined future needs
quiz.explain: You Aren't Gonna Need It: build what is needed now.

quiz.q: What is usually the best starting architecture for a small team?
quiz.explain: A modular monolith keeps things simple while staying organised.

lessons.task:
Design a small **library system** on paper:
1. Draw a C4 context diagram: users, the library system, and an external email service.
2. Split the system into three layers and list two functions in each.
3. Identify one place where dependency inversion would make testing easier.
4. Write one ADR for a decision you made (for example, which database).

lessons.title: Clean code
lessons.summary: Write code that humans can read: good names, small functions, no duplication, clear errors.

slides.title: Code is read more than written
slides.text: You write a line once. You and others read it **dozens of times**. Optimise for the reader.
slides.narration: A line of code is written once but read many times, during reviews, debugging and changes. Clean code is code that the next reader, often you six months later, understands quickly. That saves far more time than clever tricks ever do.

slides.title: Meaningful names
slides.text: Names should say **what** and **why**, not how.
slides.narration: Names are the most important documentation. Compare d with days since last login. A good name removes the need for a comment. Functions should be verbs, variables should be nouns, and booleans should read like a question.

slides.title: Small, focused functions
slides.text: A function should **do one thing**, at one level of detail. Short is good.
slides.narration: Keep functions small and focused. If you need the word and to describe what a function does, it probably does two things. Split it. Small functions are easier to name, test and reuse.

slides.title: Avoid duplication and magic numbers
slides.text: Extract repeated logic. Name constants.
slides.narration: When you copy and paste logic, every future fix has to be made in several places, and one will be forgotten. Pull repeated code into a function. Replace unexplained numbers with named constants, so readers know what eighteen or zero point two means.

slides.title: Formatting, comments and tools
slides.text:
- Follow a **style guide** (PEP 8 for Python)
- Let **formatters** and **linters** do the boring work (Ruff, Black, Prettier, ESLint)
- Comment **why**, not what
slides.narration: Consistency matters more than any particular style. Use a style guide and let tools enforce it automatically. In Python, Ruff can lint and format very quickly. Use comments to explain why something is done, because the code itself already shows what.

lessons.notes:
## Clean code checklist

- **Names** reveal intent: `elapsed_days`, not `d`.
- **Functions** are small and do one thing.
- **No duplication**: extract shared logic.
- **No magic numbers**: use named constants.
- **Early returns** instead of deep nesting.
- **Clear errors**: fail loudly with a helpful message instead of silently returning `None`.
- **Consistent formatting**, enforced by tools.
- **Comments explain why**, the code explains what.

## Guard clauses instead of nesting

```python
# Nested
def ship(order):
    if order:
        if order.paid:
            if order.items:
                send(order)

# Flat and clear
def ship(order):
    if not order or not order.paid or not order.items:
        return
    send(order)
```

## Refactoring

**Refactoring** means changing the structure of code without changing its behaviour. Do it in small steps and run the tests after each step. Common refactorings: rename, extract function, inline variable, replace magic number with constant.

## The Boy Scout rule

"Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it." Small improvements each time you touch a file keep a codebase healthy.

## Tools (Python, 2026)

- **Ruff**: very fast linter and formatter.
- **Black**: opinionated formatter.
- **mypy** or **pyright**: type checkers that use type hints.

```python
def average(scores: list[float]) -> float:
    return sum(scores) / len(scores)
```

Type hints act like documentation that tools can verify.

quiz.q: Which name is cleanest for a list of unpaid invoices?
quiz.explain: It says exactly what the variable holds.

quiz.q: What is refactoring?
options: Changing code structure without changing behaviour
quiz.explain: Refactoring improves design while keeping behaviour the same.

quiz.q: What should comments mostly explain?
quiz.explain: Code shows what; comments add the why that code cannot express.

exercise.title: Refactor the grade report
exercise.prompt:
The starter code works but is messy (bad names, magic numbers, duplication). **Rewrite it cleanly** while keeping exactly the same output.

**Input:** first line `n`, then `n` lines each with a student name and an integer score (0 to 100), separated by a space.

**Output:** for each student, in input order, print `name: score grade` where grade is `A` for 90+, `B` for 80+, `C` for 70+, `D` for 60+, otherwise `F`. Then print `Average: X` with the average rounded to 1 decimal place (format `.1f`).

Ana: 95 A
Ben: 72 C
Cai: 58 F
Average: 75.0

A: 90 A
B: 89 B
C: 60 D
D: 59 F
Average: 74.5

lessons.title: Design patterns
lessons.summary: Recognise proven solutions to common design problems: Strategy, Factory, Observer, Adapter and more.

slides.title: What is a pattern?
slides.text: A **named, reusable solution** to a common design problem. Not code to copy, but an idea to adapt.
slides.narration: A design pattern is a well known solution to a problem that keeps coming up. Patterns give teams a shared vocabulary. Saying we could use a strategy here communicates a whole design in four words. The classic catalogue comes from the Gang of Four book from 1994.

slides.title: Three families
slides.text:
- **Creational**: how objects are made (Factory, Builder, Singleton)
- **Structural**: how objects fit together (Adapter, Decorator, Facade)
- **Behavioural**: how objects talk (Strategy, Observer, Command)
slides.narration: Patterns are usually grouped into three families. Creational patterns are about creating objects. Structural patterns are about combining them. Behavioural patterns are about how they communicate and share responsibility.

slides.title: Strategy
slides.text: Swap an **algorithm** at runtime. In Python, a dict of functions is often enough.
slides.code:
def regular(total): return total
def student(total): return total * 0.8
def black_friday(total): return total * 0.5

PRICING = {'regular': regular, 'student': student,
           'black_friday': black_friday}

price = PRICING[customer_type](cart_total)
slides.narration: The strategy pattern lets you choose an algorithm at runtime. Instead of a long chain of if statements, you keep each behaviour in its own function and pick one by name. In Python, functions are values, so a dictionary of functions is a neat strategy.

slides.title: Observer
slides.text: When one object changes, **subscribers are notified** automatically.
slides.narration: The observer pattern connects a subject with many listeners. When something happens, the subject notifies every subscriber. Button click handlers in the browser and event systems in games work exactly like this.

slides.title: Factory and Adapter
slides.text:
- **Factory**: one place decides which class to create
- **Adapter**: wrap an incompatible interface so it fits yours
slides.narration: A factory centralises object creation, so the rest of the code does not need to know which concrete class it gets. An adapter wraps something with the wrong shape, like an old library, so it fits the interface your code expects. Like a travel plug adapter.

slides.title: Use with care
slides.text: Patterns solve problems. **No problem, no pattern.** Simple code beats clever architecture.
slides.narration: A word of warning. Patterns are tools, not goals. Adding patterns where there is no problem makes code harder to read. Start simple, and when you notice a recurring pain, reach for the pattern that fits.

lessons.notes:
## Pattern cheat sheet

| Pattern | Problem it solves | Everyday example |
|---------|-------------------|------------------|
| **Strategy** | Choose an algorithm at runtime | Different shipping cost rules |
| **Observer** | Notify many listeners of changes | UI events, notifications |
| **Factory** | Hide which class is created | Create a parser based on file type |
| **Adapter** | Make incompatible interfaces work together | Wrap an old payment API |
| **Decorator** | Add behaviour without changing a class | Python `@cache`, logging wrappers |
| **Facade** | Simple front for a complex subsystem | One `send_email()` hiding SMTP details |
| **Singleton** | Exactly one instance | Often better replaced by passing one object around |
| **Command** | Treat actions as objects | Undo/redo stacks |

## Strategy in Python

```python
OPERATIONS = {
    'add': lambda a, b: a + b,
    'mul': lambda a, b: a * b,
}

def apply(op, a, b):
    if op not in OPERATIONS:
        raise ValueError(f'unknown operation {op}')
    return OPERATIONS[op](a, b)
```

Adding a new operation means adding one line to the dictionary, without touching `apply`. This is the **open/closed principle** in action.

## Decorator in Python

```python
from functools import cache

@cache
def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
```

## Patterns in modern code

Many patterns are built into languages and frameworks today: iterators, decorators, dependency injection containers, and event emitters. Recognising them helps you understand library code quickly.

## Anti-patterns

Also learn the bad ones: **God object** (one class knows everything), **spaghetti code**, **copy-paste programming** and **premature optimisation**.

quiz.q: Which pattern lets you pick an algorithm at runtime?
quiz.explain: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms.

quiz.q: Click event listeners in a browser are an example of...
quiz.explain: Listeners subscribe and are notified when the event happens.

quiz.q: Which family does Adapter belong to?
quiz.explain: Adapter is about fitting objects together, a structural concern.

exercise.title: Strategy calculator
exercise.prompt:
Implement a small calculator using the **Strategy** pattern (a dictionary mapping names to functions).

**Input:** first line `n`, then `n` lines of the form `op a b` where `a` and `b` are integers and `op` is one of `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `max`.

**Output:** for each line print the result. If `op` is not known, print `unknown: op` (with the operation name).

modules.title: Working safely: Git, tests and debugging

lessons.title: Version control with Git
lessons.summary: Track every change, work on branches, and collaborate through remotes and pull requests.

slides.title: Why version control?
slides.text:
- A **history** of every change: who, what, when, why
- **Undo** mistakes safely
- **Work in parallel** without overwriting each other
slides.narration: Version control records every change to your project. You can see who changed what, when and why, go back to any earlier version, and let many people work on the same code at the same time. Git is by far the most used version control system.

slides.title: The three areas
slides.text: **Working directory** → (add) → **staging area** → (commit) → **repository**
slides.code:
git init
git status
git add app.py
git commit -m "Add login form validation"
git log --oneline
slides.narration: Git has three areas. The working directory is your files as you edit them. You choose which changes to include with git add, which puts them in the staging area. Then git commit saves a snapshot in the repository, with a message.

slides.title: Branches
slides.text: A **branch** is a movable pointer to a line of work. Create one per feature or fix.
slides.code:
git switch -c feature/password-reset
# ...edit, add, commit...
git switch main
git merge feature/password-reset
slides.narration: Branches let you work on something without disturbing the main code. Create a branch for each feature or fix, commit there, and merge it back when it is ready. Switching branches is instant.

slides.title: Remotes and pull requests
slides.text: Push to a shared **remote** (GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg...). Open a **pull request** to propose merging.
slides.code:
git push -u origin feature/password-reset
# open a pull request on the website
git pull            # get teammates' changes
slides.narration: To collaborate, you push your branch to a shared remote repository. Then you open a pull request, also called a merge request, which asks the team to review and merge your changes. Automated checks run on it too.

slides.title: Merge conflicts
slides.text: When two branches change the **same lines**, Git asks you to choose.
slides.narration: Sometimes two people edit the same lines. Git cannot guess which version is right, so it marks the conflict in the file. You edit the file to keep the correct result, remove the markers, then add and commit. Small, frequent merges keep conflicts rare.

slides.title: Good habits
slides.text:
- Small commits, clear messages
- Never commit secrets; use **.gitignore**
- Pull often, keep branches short-lived
- Undo safely: **git restore**, **git revert**
slides.narration: Commit small, related changes with messages that explain what and why. Add files such as dot env and build folders to dot gitignore. Merge often so branches stay short. And learn safe undo commands: restore discards local edits, and revert creates a new commit that undoes an old one.

lessons.notes:
## Everyday Git commands

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| Start a repo | `git init` or `git clone <url>` |
| See what changed | `git status`, `git diff` |
| Stage | `git add <file>` (or `git add -p` to pick parts) |
| Commit | `git commit -m "message"` |
| History | `git log --oneline --graph` |
| New branch | `git switch -c <name>` |
| Change branch | `git switch <name>` |
| Merge | `git merge <branch>` |
| Share | `git push`, `git pull` |
| Discard local edits | `git restore <file>` |
| Undo a pushed commit | `git revert <commit>` |

## Writing good commit messages

```
Add password reset email

Users who forget their password can now request a reset link.
The link expires after 30 minutes.
```

Many teams use **Conventional Commits**: `feat: add password reset`, `fix: handle empty cart`, `docs: update README`. Tools can generate changelogs and version numbers from them.

## Branching strategies

- **Trunk-based development**: short-lived branches merged into `main` at least daily, often with feature flags. Popular with CI/CD.
- **GitHub Flow**: branch, pull request, review, merge to `main`, deploy.
- **Git Flow**: long-lived `develop` and release branches; heavier, used for versioned products.

## .gitignore example

```
.env
__pycache__/
node_modules/
dist/
*.log
```

## If you committed a secret

Removing it in a new commit is not enough: it is still in history. **Rotate the secret immediately** (create a new key, disable the old one), then clean history if needed.

## Rebase vs merge

`git rebase` replays your commits on top of another branch for a straight history. Never rebase commits that others already pulled.

quiz.q: Which command moves changes into the staging area?
quiz.explain: git add stages changes for the next commit.

quiz.q: What is a pull request?
options: A proposal to merge a branch, with review and checks
quiz.explain: Pull (or merge) requests let the team review before merging.

quiz.q: You accidentally pushed an API key. What must you do first?
quiz.explain: Assume the key is compromised; revoke it and issue a new one.

lessons.title: Testing your code
lessons.summary: Write automated tests that prove your code works and keep it working: unit, integration, end-to-end, TDD.

slides.title: Why test?
slides.text:
Tests are code that **checks your code**.
- Catch bugs **before** users do
- Change code **without fear**
- Document how code should behave
slides.narration: An automated test is a small program that runs your code and checks the result. Tests catch bugs early, when they are cheap to fix. More importantly, they let you change and refactor code confidently, because the tests shout if you break something.

slides.title: The test pyramid
slides.text:
- Many **unit** tests (one function, fast)
- Some **integration** tests (parts together, database)
- Few **end-to-end** tests (whole app, like a user)
slides.narration: The test pyramid suggests many fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests in the middle that check parts working together, and a small number of slow end to end tests at the top that click through the real app like a user.

slides.title: A unit test with pytest
slides.text: Arrange, **Act**, Assert.
slides.narration: Here is a unit test written with pytest, the most popular Python testing tool. Each test arranges some input, acts by calling the function, and asserts the expected result. Run pytest in the terminal and it finds and runs every test automatically.

slides.title: Test the edges
slides.text: Bugs hide at **boundaries**: zero, empty, negative, very large, exactly on a limit.
slides.narration: Good tests do not only check the happy path. Bugs love boundaries: an empty list, zero, a negative number, or a value exactly on a limit like eighteen for an age check. Write a test for each, and for invalid input that should raise an error.

slides.title: Test-driven development
slides.text: **Red** (write a failing test) → **Green** (make it pass) → **Refactor**.
slides.narration: Test driven development flips the order. First write a test that fails, which is red. Then write just enough code to make it pass, which is green. Then clean up the code, refactor, while the tests protect you. Repeat in tiny steps.

lessons.notes:
## Kinds of tests

| Type | Scope | Speed | Example |
|------|-------|-------|---------|
| Unit | One function or class | Milliseconds | `is_leap_year(2024)` is `True` |
| Integration | Several parts together | Seconds | API handler writes to a test database |
| End-to-end | Whole system via the UI | Slow | Playwright logs in and buys a product |

Other useful kinds: **regression tests** (one per fixed bug), **property-based tests** (Hypothesis generates many inputs), **performance** and **security** tests.

## pytest essentials

```python
import pytest
from leap import is_leap_year

@pytest.mark.parametrize("year, expected", [
    (2024, True), (2023, False), (1900, False), (2000, True),
])
def test_leap(year, expected):
    assert is_leap_year(year) == expected

def test_rejects_negative():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        is_leap_year(-5)
```

Run with `pytest` (install with `pip install pytest`). Python also ships `unittest` in the standard library.

## What makes a good test?

- **Fast** and **independent**: tests can run in any order.
- **Repeatable**: no reliance on time, randomness or the network (use fakes/mocks).
- **One reason to fail**, with a clear name: `test_empty_cart_total_is_zero`.
- Tests **behaviour**, not private details.

## Coverage

Coverage tools (`pytest --cov`) show which lines ran during tests. High coverage is useful, but 100% coverage does not mean bug-free: you must also assert the right things.

## Judged exercises are tests

Every exercise in this editor is checked by tests: input goes in, and the output must match exactly. In the exercise below, the leap-year rules come with built-in edge cases.

quiz.q: Which tests should you have the most of?
quiz.explain: Unit tests are fast and cheap, forming the base of the pyramid.

quiz.q: What is the order in TDD?

quiz.q: Why is 1900 a good test case for a leap-year function?

quiz.explain: Century years are the boundary where naive logic fails.

lessons.title: Debugging
lessons.summary: Find and fix bugs systematically: reproduce, read errors, isolate, use a debugger, fix and prevent.

slides.title: Bugs are normal
slides.text: Every developer writes bugs. The skill is finding them **calmly and systematically**, not guessing.
slides.narration: Every programmer writes bugs, every day. What separates beginners from professionals is not fewer bugs, it is a calm, systematic way of finding them. Random changes and hoping is the slowest way to debug.

slides.title: The debugging loop
slides.text:
1. **Reproduce** reliably
2. **Read** the error and stack trace
3. **Form a hypothesis**
4. **Test** it (print, debugger)
5. **Fix**, then add a test so it never returns
slides.narration: Follow a loop. First make the bug happen reliably. Read the error message carefully. Guess a cause, then test that guess with prints or a debugger. When you find it, fix it and write a regression test so the bug can never sneak back.

slides.title: Read the traceback
slides.text: Python tells you the **file**, **line** and **error type**. Read from the **bottom up**.
slides.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "report.py", line 9, in <module>
    print(average([]))
  File "report.py", line 3, in average
    return sum(nums) / len(nums)
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
slides.narration: Error messages are your friends. In Python, read the traceback from the bottom. The last line tells you the error type and message. The lines above show the chain of calls that led there, ending with the exact line that failed.

slides.title: Tools of the trade
slides.text:
- **print** / **logging** to see values
- A **debugger**: breakpoints, step, inspect variables (`breakpoint()` in Python)
- **Rubber duck**: explain the code out loud
- **git bisect** to find the commit that broke it
slides.narration: Printing values is simple and effective. A debugger is even better: set a breakpoint, pause the program, and inspect every variable step by step. Explaining your code line by line to a rubber duck, or a colleague, often reveals the bug. And git bisect can find which commit introduced it.

slides.title: Classic bug types
slides.text:
- **Off-by-one** (range end, index 0)
- **Wrong type** ("5" vs 5)
- **Mutating shared data**
- **Unhandled empty / None input**
- **Wrong initial value** (max starting at 0)
slides.narration: Some bugs appear again and again. Off by one errors in loops and ranges. Mixing up text and numbers. Changing a list that another part of the code also uses. Forgetting empty input. And starting a maximum at zero, which breaks when all numbers are negative. The exercise in this lesson has exactly that kind of bug.

lessons.notes:
## A systematic method

1. **Reproduce**: find the exact input and steps. Write them down.
2. **Simplify**: shrink the input until the bug still happens with the smallest case.
3. **Read** the error message and traceback (bottom line first).
4. **Hypothesise**: "I think `total` is wrong because the loop skips the last item."
5. **Experiment**: print values or step with a debugger to confirm or reject.
6. **Fix** the root cause, not the symptom.
7. **Protect**: add a test for that exact case.

## Common Python errors

| Error | Usually means |
|-------|---------------|
| `NameError` | Typo or variable used before it exists |
| `TypeError` | Wrong type, e.g. `"5" + 1` |
| `IndexError` | List index past the end (off-by-one) |
| `KeyError` | Missing dictionary key |
| `AttributeError` | Calling a method that does not exist (often on `None`) |
| `ZeroDivisionError` | Dividing by zero, often an empty list |

## Using the Python debugger

```python
def total(prices):
    result = 0
    for p in prices:
        breakpoint()   # pauses here; type n (next), p result, c (continue)
        result += p
    return result
```

IDEs (VS Code, PyCharm) offer the same with clickable breakpoints.

## Logging instead of print in real apps

```python
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log.info("order %s total %.2f", order_id, total)
```

Logs stay in production code at controlled levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR) and help debug problems on servers you cannot pause.

## Production debugging

In live systems, use logs, metrics and traces (observability), plus error trackers that collect stack traces automatically.

quiz.q: What is the first step in debugging?
quiz.explain: If you cannot reproduce it, you cannot confirm a fix.

quiz.q: Where should you start reading a Python traceback?
quiz.explain: The last line names the error; the line just above shows where it happened.

quiz.q: Why add a test after fixing a bug?
options: To make sure the bug never comes back unnoticed
quiz.explain: A regression test guards against the same bug returning.

exercise.prompt:

**Input:** first line `n` (n ≥ 1), second line `n` integers separated by spaces (they can be negative).

**Output:** three lines: `min: X`, `max: Y`, `count above average: Z`, where Z counts the numbers strictly greater than the average.
exercise.starter:
n = int(input())
nums = input().split()
lo = 0
hi = 0
for i in range(1, n):
    x = nums[i]
    if x < lo:
        lo = x
    if x > hi:
        hi = x
avg = sum(int(v) for v in nums) / n

    if x > hi:
        hi = x

above = sum(1 for v in nums if v > avg)
print('min:', lo)
print('max:', hi)
print('count above average:', above)

lessons.title: Agile and Scrum
lessons.summary: Understand the agile mindset and how Scrum and Kanban organise a team's work week by week.

slides.title: The Agile Manifesto (2001)
slides.text:
We value:
- **Individuals and interactions** over processes and tools
- **Working software** over comprehensive documentation
- **Customer collaboration** over contract negotiation
- **Responding to change** over following a plan
slides.narration: In 2001 a group of developers wrote the Agile Manifesto. It values people and conversations, working software, collaboration with customers, and responding to change. The things on the right still matter, but the things on the left matter more.

slides.title: Scrum roles
slides.text:
- **Product Owner**: owns the backlog, decides priority
- **Scrum Master**: coaches the process, removes blockers
- **Developers**: everyone who builds the increment
slides.narration: Scrum is the most popular agile framework. It has three accountabilities. The product owner decides what is most valuable to build next. The scrum master helps the team use scrum well and removes obstacles. The developers, which includes testers and designers, do the work.

slides.title: The sprint
slides.text:
A fixed time box, usually **1 to 4 weeks**:
1. **Sprint Planning**
2. **Daily Scrum** (15 min)
3. **Sprint Review** (demo)
4. **Retrospective** (improve)
slides.narration: Work happens in sprints, fixed time boxes of one to four weeks. It starts with sprint planning, where the team picks a sprint goal and backlog items. Every day there is a short daily scrum. At the end, the team demos the work in the sprint review and improves its way of working in the retrospective.

slides.title: Artifacts
slides.text:
- **Product Backlog**: ordered list of everything wanted
- **Sprint Backlog**: what we commit to this sprint
- **Increment**: a usable, tested piece of product
- **Definition of Done**: the quality bar
slides.narration: Scrum has three artifacts. The product backlog is the ordered list of all wanted work. The sprint backlog is the plan for this sprint. The increment is the usable result. The definition of done is a shared checklist, for example reviewed, tested and documented, that every item must meet.

slides.title: Kanban
slides.text:
Visualise work on a **board**: To do → Doing → Review → Done.
**Limit work in progress** and keep it flowing.
slides.narration: Kanban is a lighter approach. All work is visible on a board with columns. The key rule is to limit work in progress: the team finishes things before starting new ones. Many teams mix Scrum and Kanban ideas.

lessons.notes:
## Agile principles in practice

- Deliver working software **frequently**.
- Welcome **changing requirements**, even late.
- Business people and developers work **together daily**.
- Reflect regularly and **improve** how the team works.
- **Simplicity**: maximise the work not done.

## Scrum at a glance

| Event | When | Purpose |
|-------|------|---------|
| Sprint Planning | Start of sprint | Choose a sprint goal and items |
| Daily Scrum | Every day, 15 min | Inspect progress toward the goal, adapt the plan |
| Sprint Review | End of sprint | Show the increment, get feedback |
| Retrospective | After review | Improve process and teamwork |

## Estimation

Teams often estimate with **story points** (relative size: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13) using **planning poker**. The goal is shared understanding, not precise hours. **Velocity**, the points finished per sprint, helps forecast but should never be used to compare teams.

## Kanban essentials

```
| To do | Doing (max 3) | Review (max 2) | Done |
|-------|---------------|----------------|------|
| A     | B, C          | D              | E, F |
```

Measure **lead time** (from request to done) and **cycle time** (from start to done). Lower and more predictable is better.

## Common pitfalls

- "Agile" as an excuse for no planning or no documentation.
- Daily scrums that turn into long status reports for a manager.
- Sprints full of unfinished work because the definition of done is ignored.
- Skipping retrospectives: then nothing improves.

## Beyond the team

Large organisations scale agile with frameworks such as SAFe or LeSS, and combine it with **DevOps** practices so finished work actually reaches users quickly.

quiz.q: Who decides the priority of the product backlog in Scrum?
quiz.explain: The Product Owner is accountable for ordering the backlog.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a retrospective?
quiz.explain: Retrospectives inspect and adapt the team's process.

quiz.q: What is the key rule of Kanban?
quiz.explain: WIP limits keep work flowing and expose bottlenecks.

lessons.task:
Run a one-week personal "sprint":
1. Write a product backlog of at least eight items for a small project (e.g. a recipe app), ordered by value.
2. Estimate each with story points (1, 2, 3, 5, 8).
3. Choose a sprint goal and the items that fit it.
4. Track progress on a Kanban board (paper or app) with a WIP limit of 2.
5. At the end, write a short retrospective: what went well, what to improve, one action.

lessons.title: Code review and documentation
lessons.summary: Give and receive helpful code reviews, and write documentation people actually read.

slides.title: Why review code?
slides.text:
- Catch bugs and security issues
- **Share knowledge** across the team
- Keep the codebase **consistent**
- Mentor and learn
slides.narration: In code review, a teammate reads your changes before they are merged. It catches bugs and security problems, but the bigger benefit is shared knowledge. More people understand each part of the system, and everyone learns from each other.

slides.title: Making a reviewable change
slides.text:
- **Small** pull requests (a few hundred lines max)
- A clear **description**: what, why, how to test
- Tests included, checks green
- Review your own diff first
slides.narration: Make your changes easy to review. Keep pull requests small and focused. Write a description that explains what changed, why, and how to test it. Make sure automated checks pass, and read your own diff before asking anyone else.

slides.title: Giving good feedback
slides.text: Be **kind, specific and clear** about importance.
slides.code:
Blocking: this query builds SQL from user input;
please use a parameter to avoid injection.

Suggestion: could `calc` be renamed `monthly_total`?

Nit: extra blank line.

Nice: the new tests cover the empty-cart case.
slides.narration: When reviewing, comment on the code, never the person. Be specific and suggest an alternative. Mark how important each comment is, so the author knows what must change and what is just a nitpick. And say what you like too.

slides.title: Documentation that helps
slides.text:
- **README**: what, why, install, run, test
- **Docstrings** for public functions
- **ADRs** for big decisions
- **API docs**, changelog
slides.narration: Documentation is for the next person. Every project needs a README explaining what it is and how to run it. Public functions get docstrings. Important decisions get short decision records. Keep docs close to the code, in the same repository, so they are updated together.

slides.title: Docstrings in Python
slides.text: Explain purpose, arguments, return value and errors.
slides.code:
def price_with_vat(net: float, rate: float = 0.2) -> float:
    """Return the gross price including VAT.

    Args:
        net: price before tax, must be >= 0.
        rate: VAT rate as a fraction (0.2 = 20%).

    Raises:
        ValueError: if net is negative.
    """
slides.narration: In Python, a docstring is a string right after a function definition. Tools and editors show it as help. Describe what the function does, its arguments, what it returns and what errors it can raise.

lessons.notes:
## Reviewer checklist

1. **Correctness**: does it do what the story asks? Edge cases?
2. **Tests**: are there tests, and do they test behaviour?
3. **Security**: input validation, secrets, permissions.
4. **Readability**: names, function size, comments explain why.
5. **Design**: fits the architecture, no needless complexity.
6. **Performance**: obvious waste (queries in loops, huge allocations).

Leave style issues to **automated formatters and linters**, so humans focus on logic.

## Comment labels

Many teams prefix comments: **blocking**, **suggestion**, **question**, **nit**, **praise**. This removes guesswork about what must change.

## Receiving feedback

- Assume good intent; the review is about the code.
- Ask questions when unclear.
- It is fine to disagree with reasons; agree on a decision and move on.
- Say thanks.

## AI-assisted review

In 2026 many teams run AI review tools that flag likely bugs before a human looks. They are helpful, but a human reviewer still owns the decision to merge.

## A good README skeleton

```markdown
# Recipe Box
Save and search your family recipes.

## Run locally
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python app.py

## Test
pytest

## Contributing
See CONTRIBUTING.md
```

## Kinds of documentation (Diátaxis)

- **Tutorials**: learning by doing.
- **How-to guides**: steps for a specific task.
- **Reference**: exact details (API, config).
- **Explanation**: background and reasons.

Knowing which kind you are writing keeps docs focused.

quiz.q: What is a good size for a pull request?
quiz.explain: Small PRs are reviewed faster and more thoroughly.

quiz.q: A reviewer comment should focus on...
quiz.explain: Specific, kind feedback about the code is most helpful.

quiz.q: What belongs in a README?
options: What the project is, how to install, run and test it
quiz.explain: A README gets a newcomer from zero to running.

exercise.title: Docstring checker
exercise.prompt:
A team requires every function to have a docstring. Write a tiny checker.

**Input:** Python source code (several lines, until end of input).

**Output:** for every line that starts (after optional spaces) with `def `, look at the **next non-empty line**. If it starts (after spaces) with `"""` print `name: ok`, otherwise print `name: missing docstring`, where `name` is the function name (text between `def ` and `(`). If no functions are found print `no functions`.
exercise.starter:
import sys

lines = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
# find def lines and check the next non-empty line
exercise.solution:
import sys

lines = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
found = False
for i, line in enumerate(lines):
    stripped = line.strip()
    if not stripped.startswith('def '):
        continue
    found = True
    name = stripped[4:stripped.index('(')].strip()
    following = ''
    for nxt in lines[i + 1:]:
        if nxt.strip():
            following = nxt.strip()
            break
    print(f'{name}: ' + ('ok' if following.startswith('"""') else 'missing docstring'))
if not found:
    print('no functions')

lessons.title: CI/CD and releasing software
lessons.summary: Automate building, testing and deploying with continuous integration and delivery pipelines.

slides.title: The old way and the new way
slides.text:
**Old**: big releases every few months, long nights, lots of bugs.
**New**: small changes, **automatically tested and deployed**, many times a day.
slides.narration: Years ago teams released software a few times a year in big, scary launches. Today, good teams release small changes many times a day. The secret is automation: every change is built, tested and deployed by a pipeline.

slides.title: CI: continuous integration
slides.text: Every push triggers: **install → lint → test → build**. Broken? Fix it first.
slides.narration: Continuous integration means everyone merges small changes into the main branch often, and every change is checked automatically. A CI server installs dependencies, runs the linter and the tests, and builds the app. If something fails, fixing it becomes the top priority.

slides.title: A GitHub Actions workflow
slides.text: Pipelines are defined as **code** in the repository.
slides.code:
name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.13" }
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: ruff check .
      - run: pytest
slides.narration: Here is a simple pipeline for GitHub Actions. It runs on every push and pull request, sets up Python, installs dependencies, and runs Ruff and pytest. GitLab CI and others use very similar files.

slides.title: CD: delivery and deployment
slides.text:
- **Continuous delivery**: every change is *ready* to release (one click)
- **Continuous deployment**: every passing change *goes live* automatically
- Staging → production
slides.narration: CD can mean two things. Continuous delivery means every passing change is ready to release with one click. Continuous deployment goes further and releases it automatically. Changes usually pass through a staging environment that mirrors production first.

slides.title: Releasing safely
slides.text:
- **Feature flags**: ship code turned off
- **Canary / rolling** releases
- **Rollback** quickly
- **Semantic versioning**: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
slides.narration: Safe releases use a few tricks. Feature flags let you deploy code switched off and enable it later. Canary releases send a small share of users to the new version first. Always be able to roll back fast. And version releases with semantic versioning, where the major number signals breaking changes.

lessons.notes:
## Pipeline stages

1. **Checkout** the code.
2. **Install** dependencies (with a lock file for repeatable builds).
3. **Lint and format check** (Ruff, ESLint).
4. **Type check** (mypy, pyright, tsc).
5. **Test** (unit, then integration).
6. **Security scans**: dependency vulnerabilities, secret scanning.
7. **Build** an artifact (package, container image).
8. **Deploy** to staging, run smoke tests.
9. **Deploy** to production (manual approval or automatic).

## Popular tools (2026)

GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, Jenkins, CircleCI, Buildkite, Azure Pipelines. Containers (Docker) and infrastructure as code (Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi) make environments repeatable.

## Semantic Versioning

`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, for example `2.4.1`:

| Change | Bump | Example |
|--------|------|---------|
| Breaking API change | MAJOR, reset others | 2.4.1 → 3.0.0 |
| New backwards-compatible feature | MINOR, reset patch | 2.4.1 → 2.5.0 |
| Bug fix | PATCH | 2.4.1 → 2.4.2 |

## DORA metrics

Research by the DORA program measures delivery performance with: **deployment frequency**, **lead time for changes**, **change failure rate** and **time to restore service**. Elite teams deploy on demand and recover in under an hour.

## Keep the pipeline fast

Slow pipelines get skipped. Cache dependencies, run tests in parallel, and keep the slow end-to-end suite small. A good target is feedback in under ten minutes.

## Production is part of the job

After deploy, **monitor**: logs, metrics, traces and alerts. "You build it, you run it" means the team that writes the code also watches it in production.

quiz.q: What does continuous integration mean?
options: Merging small changes often, each automatically built and tested
quiz.explain: CI checks every change automatically and keeps main healthy.

quiz.q: Version 1.4.2 gets a backwards-compatible new feature. New version?
quiz.explain: A MINOR bump resets PATCH to 0.

quiz.q: What is a feature flag?
options: A switch that turns deployed code on or off without redeploying
quiz.explain: Flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature.

exercise.title: Semantic version bump
exercise.prompt:
Write the version-bump step of a release pipeline.

lessons.title: Growing your career as a developer
lessons.summary: Plan your path: skills, portfolio, open source, interviews, and lifelong learning in an AI-assisted world.

slides.title: Many paths
slides.text:
- Front-end, back-end, full-stack
- Mobile, games, embedded
- Data, ML/AI engineering
- DevOps, platform, SRE, security
- QA / test automation
slides.narration: Software development has many paths. You can build user interfaces, servers, mobile apps, games or devices. You can work with data and AI, keep systems running as a platform or reliability engineer, or specialise in security or test automation. You do not need to choose forever on day one.

slides.title: T-shaped skills
slides.text: **Broad** basics (Git, testing, SQL, web, Linux) + **deep** skill in one area.
slides.narration: A useful model is the T shape. The top bar is broad: everyone benefits from Git, testing, SQL, how the web works and the command line. The vertical bar is depth in one area that you become really good at.

slides.title: Show, don't tell
slides.text:
- **Portfolio**: 2 to 3 finished projects with READMEs and tests
- **Open source** contributions
- Write about what you learn
- Clean public Git history
slides.narration: Employers want evidence. Two or three finished, well documented projects beat twenty half done tutorials. Contributing to open source, even documentation fixes, shows you can work with others. Writing short posts about what you learned shows communication skills.

slides.title: Interviews
slides.text:
- **Coding**: data structures, problem solving, talking through ideas
- **System design** (for more senior roles)
- **Behavioural**: teamwork, conflict, learning (STAR method)
slides.narration: Interviews usually include coding problems, where explaining your thinking matters as much as the answer. More senior roles add system design. Behavioural questions ask about real situations, and the STAR method helps: situation, task, action, result.

slides.title: Keep learning
slides.text:
- Read code, docs and changelogs
- Use AI assistants **as a tutor, not a crutch**
- Find mentors and community
- Rest: careers are marathons
slides.narration: Technology keeps changing, so learning never stops. Read other peoples code and official documentation. Use AI assistants to explain and to speed up, but make sure you understand everything you ship. Find mentors and communities. And look after yourself, because a career is a marathon, not a sprint.

lessons.notes:
## Building blocks every developer needs

- **A language deeply** (e.g. Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, C#, Go).
- **Git** and pull-request workflow.
- **Testing** and debugging.
- **SQL** and basic data modelling.
- **The command line** and basic Linux.
- **How the web and HTTP work**.
- **Communication**: writing clear issues, PR descriptions and docs.

## Portfolio checklist

For each project:

1. Solves a real (even small) problem.
2. README with screenshots, how to run, tech choices.
3. Tests and a CI badge.
4. Deployed or easy to run.
5. Honest about what you built and what you learned.

## Getting into open source

Look for issues labelled `good first issue` or `help wanted`. Read `CONTRIBUTING.md`, start with documentation or small fixes, and be patient and polite with maintainers.

## Interview preparation

- Practise problems by explaining your reasoning out loud.
- Review core data structures: arrays, hash maps, stacks, queues, trees, graphs.
- Prepare 4 to 5 STAR stories (a bug you solved, a conflict, a failure, a success).
- Ask the interviewers questions about their team, process and code review culture.

## Working with AI tools in 2026

AI assistants write a lot of first-draft code. Your value shifts toward **understanding problems, designing systems, reviewing, testing and taking responsibility**. Everything in this course, from requirements to CI/CD, is how you check and guide that work.

## Levels

Junior → mid → senior → staff/principal (or engineering manager). Growth is less about years and more about scope: from completing tasks, to owning features, to shaping systems and helping others grow.

quiz.q: What does "T-shaped" mean for a developer?
options: Broad basic skills plus deep expertise in one area
quiz.explain: Broad foundations plus one deep specialty.

quiz.q: What does the STAR method stand for?
quiz.explain: STAR structures behavioural interview answers.

quiz.q: What is a healthy way to use AI coding assistants?
options: Ship generated code without reading it
Use them to learn and speed up, while understanding and testing everything you ship
quiz.explain: You remain responsible for code you merge.

lessons.task:
Write your personal development plan:
1. Choose a target role (e.g. junior back-end developer).
2. List your current skills and the five most important gaps.
3. Plan two portfolio projects that close those gaps, each with a README, tests and CI.
4. Find one open-source project and one `good first issue` you could try.
5. Write two STAR stories from school, work or personal projects.
